Amazon River. The Amazon River is the world's largest by discharge volume, flowing approximately 4,000 miles through the heart of South America before emptying into the Atlantic. Originating in the Andes and draining an immense basin spanning multiple countries (primarily Brazil), it is the lifeblood of the Amazon rainforest, sustaining extraordinary biodiversity and indigenous cultures. The Amazon system is a critical regulator of global climate and weather patterns. First, discharges roughly 209,000 cubic meters of water per second into the Atlantic—about 10% of all river water entering the world's oceans. Additionally, the basin covers approximately 2.1 million square miles, spanning nine countries but primarily Brazil; it represents roughly 10% of all tropical rainforest on Earth. Equally important, the river is navigable for most of its length, serving as the primary highway for communities in the interior; steamboats and canoes are lifelines for remote settlements. Worth noting is home to over 1,100 fish species and countless undiscovered organisms; the rainforest canopy harbors biodiversity surpassing most terrestrial ecosystems. Another key fact: indigenous peoples, including the Yanomami, have inhabited the basin for millennia, developing sophisticated ecological knowledge and sustainable harvesting practices. Less well known, the Amazon produces roughly 20% of the world's oxygen (often exaggerated in pop culture, but significant); deforestation threatens this carbon sink and accelerates climate change. The detail most often asked about: deforestation, cattle ranching, dam construction, and illegal gold mining have destroyed roughly 20% of the original forest; tipping points toward savannization are a major climate concern.
